A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Proxy Target study and are readable throughout. v1 ends after the references despite referring to an appendix; v2 supplies Appendix A. This supports comparison of the added documentation without assuming that the underlying implementation changed.

before.justification: v1 reports the authors' TD3-based MuJoCo experiments, including learning curves, five-seed return comparisons, target-output diagnostics and energy estimates.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds conversion-baseline results, firing-rate measurements and detailed results for the ANN control.

M1.justification: Both versions replace the spiking target actor with a continuous proxy trained through squared output-matching loss and repeated gradient updates, while retaining Polyak updates for the critic. The new pseudocode and appendix disclose implementation choices, including the proxy update schedule, without establishing a redesign.

E1.justification: Both evaluate InvertedDoublePendulum-v4, Ant-v4, HalfCheetah-v4, Hopper-v4 and Walker2d-v4. The added comparator and appendix results use these same tasks; the environment illustration introduces no additional coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds the ANN-SNN conversion method attributed to Bu et al. (2025). The existing comparators remain: Tang et al. (2021), Zhang et al. (2022) and Chen et al. (2024a) in v1 correspond to pop-SAN, MDC-SAN and ILC-SAN in v2.

E3.justification: The energy-estimation assumption changes from 12.5 pJ per FLOP in v1 to 3.97 pJ per MAC in v2; the SOP cost remains 77 fJ. The added conversion comparator uses 100 simulation steps. Newly specified settings for retained experiments are documentation additions, not evidence that those experiments were rerun differently.

E4.justification: v2 Section 5.6 adds a limited sparsity comparison: average firing rates are 32% for PT-LIF and 33% for vanilla LIF. The target-output/MSE diagnostics, neuron comparisons and ANN control already exist in v1; Appendix A.6 mainly provides more detailed displays of those retained analyses.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 5(b) presents the ANN control through aggregate curves without uncertainty bands. v2 Figure 8 and Table 11 additionally report task-level variability for that existing control. Five-seed reporting, one-standard-deviation table entries and half-standard-deviation curve bands remain the general practice; no increase in runs or new significance test is established.

E6.justification: Shared Table 1 returns and APGs are unchanged. v2 adds conversion results with -21.11% APG and detailed proxy-ANN results with -8.38% APG. Table 2 replaces the ANN energy estimates under different cost assumptions, reporting an average of 281.78 nJ versus 886.33 nJ in v1; however, v2's listed task values actually average 241.80 nJ. SNN energy entries remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 adds Theorem 1 and its Appendix A.1 proof: under differentiability, a proxy's output change vanishes as its learning rate approaches zero. This is a limited local result, not an RL convergence guarantee. The appendix also supplies explicit SAN and neuron mathematics, while the original proxy-loss derivation remains.

C1.justification: The main claims remain the target-update mismatch, its remedy through a continuous imitation-trained proxy, improved stability and performance, no deployment overhead, and simple LIF neurons surpassing ANN counterparts. The abstract and introduction retain the headline improvement of up to 32%.

C2.justification: v1 explains LIF's advantage through the difficulty of approximating more complex neuron dynamics. v2 Section 5.4 instead argues that the bottleneck shifts to the RL algorithm once SNNs surpass ANNs. v2 also removes the energy discussion's 'more than two orders of magnitude' assertion and acknowledges task-dependent performance. The simulation-only limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 substantially fills the documentation absent from v1's referenced appendix. Algorithms 1–3 and Appendices A.2–A.5 specify propagation, proxy widths and learning rates, K=3 updates, neuron parameters, TD3 settings, state/action normalization and RTX 3090/Xeon hardware. The abstract also adds a code-access link. These are disclosures rather than demonstrated implementation changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds references covering ANN-SNN conversion, direct spiking RL, off-policy algorithms and NPU energy estimation, including Bu, Cao, Sun and Millar works. It removes the noisy-SAN and Qiao references. The related-work categories and central positioning around adapting RL to SNN dynamics remain substantially the same.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, preliminaries and methodology undergo extensive rewriting and clarification. v2 distinguishes training from simulation steps, corrects terminology and cross-references, and divides the former performance-analysis narrative into Sections 5.2–5.6. It also adds structured appendices and a conference checklist.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands visual documentation with an environment illustration, three algorithm boxes, parameter tables and supplementary result displays. Existing learning and stability plots are retained and renumbered; Figure 1's update labels change. Table 1 gains a comparator row, Table 2 adds operation counts, and Appendix A.6 both regroups existing scores and displays detailed ANN-control results.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially remedies v1's missing reproducibility material through explicit architectures, hyperparameters, preprocessing and training procedures in Appendices A.2–A.5. The conversion comparison and detailed ANN control also make the evidence easier to assess. These gains outweigh localized inconsistencies: Table 2's ANN average disagrees with its entries, and Algorithm 3 uses current states in its Bellman target despite Equation 2 specifying next states. The improvement is principally in reproducibility and inspectability, not higher shared performance or a general convergence guarantee.
